title: FedRAMP OSCAL September 30 Mandate: What It Means for AI Systems — Council of AI Compliance Guide
context: 2026-08-31 engine cycle — Effective September 30, 2026, FedRAMP requires all cloud service providers to submit authorization packages in OSCAL (Open Security Controls Assessment Language) format. For AI systems seeking FedRAMP authorization (including GPAI models deployed on US government infrastructure), this means every security control, assessment result, and plan of action must be machine-readable. The Council of AI verified measurement credential maps directly to OSCAL component-definition and assessment-results models.
body: The Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) OSCAL mandate takes effect September 30, 2026. After this date, all new and renewing FedRAMP authorization packages must be submitted in OSCAL format — XML, JSON, or YAML adhering to the NIST OSCAL specification. This is not just a paperwork format change; it is a structural shift toward machine-readable, continuously assessable compliance evidence. For AI systems — particularly general-purpose AI models deployed in US federal environments — three OSCAL layers matter. (1) System Security Plan (SSP): the OSCAL SSP model must describe the AI system's boundary, including model serving endpoints, training pipelines, and data provenance controls. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 controls mapped to AI-specific risks (data poisoning, model inversion, adversarial prompting) must be traceable through the OSCAL component-definition format. (2) Assessment Results: the OSCAL assessment-results model must capture the outcome of every security control test. The Council of AI verified measurement credential provides an Ed25519-signed assessment result that can be embedded directly into an OSCAL observation: a model's performance on the 14-axis measurement board (detector interop, privacy, governance, jailbreak resistance, etc.) becomes a machine-readable, independently verifiable finding within the FedRAMP package. (3) Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M): the OSCAL POA&M model must track remediation of any control gaps. The Council of AI containment index — a signed, append-only incident log — serves as a continuous monitoring feed that updates the POA&M in near-real-time: if a new jailbreak vector emerges or a model's refusal rate degrades, the index records it, and the POA&M reflects the delta. The September 30 deadline is not the end; it is the start of continuous machine-readable authorization. Practitioners preparing AI systems for FedRAMP should treat the OSCAL component-definition schema as their primary compliance artifact and embed Council of AI signed measurements as the evidence layer.
